newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - DUTCH UNEMPLOYMENT TO FALL FURTHER IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - DUTCH UNEMPLOYMENT TO FALL FURTHER IN 1997.

text.p: Burgeoning jobs growth,
comparable to that of the 1960s economic boom, will further
reduce Dutch unemployment next year, according to the 1997
budget presented to parliament on Tuesday.
Employment is expected to continue to outstrip labour market
supply, with over 100,000 jobs being created this year and next,
compared with annual labour force growth of some 70,000 people.
As a result the three-party coalition government's goal of
creating 350,000 new jobs during its term of office will be
realised in 1997 -- a year ahead of schedule -- Finance Minister
Gerrit Zalm told a pre-budget news briefing.
"Last year (1995) showed a decline in the number of benefit
claimants of working age for the first time in 25 years," Zalm
told reporters.
"This year the trend has continued and in 1997 there will be
90,000 fewer people dependent on social security than in 1994."
The government's Central Planning Bureau forecasts that the
number of unemployed people will fall to 465,000 in 1997 from
500,000 this year, corresponding to a drop in internationally
standardised unemployment to 5.25 percent from 6.0 percent.
But the government remains concerned about the relatively
high level of the long-term unemployed, out of work for longer
than a year, who account for 53 percent of the jobless total.
The 1997 budget includes various measures aimed at getting
more of the low-skilled long-term unemployed back to work,
providing financial incentives both to employers and to those
who return to work after a long spell outside the jobs market.
